task_1.title: Eliminate invalid escape sequence warnings in Jinja2 2.9.4
task_1.description: Version 2.9.4 removes library-originated invalid escape sequence deprecation warnings that could appear on Python runtimes with warnings enabled, while preserving existing template lexing and token-processing behavior.

synthesized_requirement.problem_statement: Ensure that upgrading from 2.9.3 to 2.9.4 no longer emits library-originated invalid escape sequence deprecation warnings during normal Jinja2 import and template-processing usage, without changing existing lexer, token stream, or raw/block/variable parsing behavior.

expectation.grounded: On Python versions that report invalid escape sequences, importing and using Jinja2 components such as `jinja2.lexer.Lexer`, `jinja2.lexer.TokenStream`, `jinja2.ext.Extension.filter_stream`, `jinja2.runtime.Context`, and `jinja2.nodes.Compare` should no longer produce `DeprecationWarning` for invalid escape sequences originating from Jinja2 string literals. The observable tokenization behavior for block endings, variable endings, and `raw` blocks must remain unchanged.
expectation.conceptual: The upgrade should make Jinja2 clean to use in warning-sensitive environments by removing deprecation warnings caused by the library's own string literals, while leaving template parsing and extension-facing token behavior functionally the same.

constraints.grounded: Do not change the public contracts of token streams, extension stream filtering, context access, or expression comparison APIs. Preserve existing lexer recognition of block delimiters, variable delimiters, whitespace control markers, and `raw` block termination semantics; the change should only affect warning emission from library-defined string literals.
constraints.conceptual: The fix must be non-breaking: it should only remove spurious warnings from the library itself and must not alter how templates are interpreted or how existing integrations interact with Jinja2.

behavior: Jinja2 should stop emitting invalid escape sequence `DeprecationWarning`s from its own module string literals in warning-enabled Python environments.
Using lexer-driven parsing for block tags, variable tags, and `raw` blocks should continue to produce the same parsing results as before the upgrade.

APIs that expose or consume token streams, including extension token filtering, should remain behaviorally compatible while no longer contributing invalid escape sequence warnings from library internals.
acceptance_criteria: When an application imports and uses Jinja2 under a Python runtime that reports invalid escape sequences with warnings enabled, it should not emit invalid escape sequence `DeprecationWarning`s originating from Jinja2 modules.
When templates use standard block delimiters, variable delimiters, whitespace control markers, and `raw` blocks, they should be tokenized and parsed the same way after upgrading to 2.9.4.

When extensions process a `TokenStream` through `Extension.filter_stream`, the stream contract and observable token-processing behavior should remain unchanged apart from the absence of library-originated invalid escape sequence warnings.

task_2.title: Invalidate stale bytecode caches after upgrading to 2.9.4
task_2.description: Jinja2 2.9.4 corrects a missed bytecode cache version bump so persisted template bytecode from the previous cache generation is no longer reused after upgrade. Older cache entries should be treated as stale and transparently regenerated, preserving normal template rendering while avoiding reuse of outdated compiled artifacts.

synthesized_requirement.problem_statement: Ensure that upgrading to Jinja2 2.9.4 invalidates previously persisted bytecode cache entries from the older cache generation so stale compiled templates are not reused.

expectation.grounded: Jinja2 2.9.4 should use a new bytecode cache version in `jinja2.bccache`. Any `BytecodeCache` backend that encounters entries written with the prior cache version should treat them as invalid, avoid loading that stale bytecode, and regenerate fresh compiled template bytecode under the new cache version.
expectation.conceptual: After the upgrade, old on-disk or external template bytecode caches should no longer be trusted automatically. The template engine should discard outdated cached bytecode and rebuild it transparently, while continuing to use caching normally for newly generated entries.

constraints.grounded: Do not change the public bytecode cache usage model or require callers to adopt new APIs. Cache invalidation should be limited to entries from the older cache version, and once regenerated, cache entries produced by 2.9.4 should remain reusable under the same release line without changing template rendering semantics.
constraints.conceptual: Treat this as a compatibility-preserving cache reset rather than a rendering feature change. Existing applications should continue to work without configuration changes, apart from a one-time rebuild of stale cached templates.

behavior: The bytecode cache version increases from 2 to 3.
Persisted bytecode cache entries created with the previous cache version are no longer considered valid after upgrading to 2.9.4.
When an outdated cache entry is encountered, Jinja2 falls back to recompiling the template instead of reusing the stale cached bytecode.
New cache entries generated after the upgrade are associated with the new cache version and can be reused normally by the upgraded library.
acceptance_criteria: When an application upgrades from Jinja2 2.9.3 to 2.9.4 while reusing an existing persisted bytecode cache, templates backed only by old cache entries should be recompiled rather than loaded from those stale entries.
When templates are rendered again after the upgrade has regenerated their cached bytecode, the regenerated cache entries should be reused normally.
Applications using Jinja2 bytecode caching should continue to render templates without changing their bytecode cache API usage or cache backend configuration.

task_3.title: Fix filtered loop scoping regression in Jinja2 templates
task_3.description: Jinja2 2.9.4 fixes a regression in filtered for-loops where loop filter expressions could be evaluated with incorrect scoping, causing template rendering failures instead of normal filtered iteration. The update restores correct rendering for filtered loops, including recursive cases that depend on values from the surrounding template context.

synthesized_requirement.problem_statement: Ensure that templates using filtered for-loops continue to render correctly when the filter expression references values from the surrounding template scope, including recursive loops.

expectation.grounded: Jinja2 `for` loops that use an inline filter condition must compile and render with correct variable scoping for the loop target and any enclosing context variables used by the condition. Recursive filtered loops must render matching items without raising `NameError` or other free-variable lookup failures caused by incorrect scoping. The same corrected behavior must apply in synchronous and asynchronous template execution.
expectation.conceptual: Filtered loops should behave as normal iteration with a condition: items that satisfy the condition are rendered, items that do not are skipped, and variables from the surrounding template remain available while the condition is evaluated.

constraints.grounded: The fix must preserve existing `for`-loop semantics for recursion, loop variables, async iteration, and optional `else` handling. Unfiltered loops must not change behavior, and filtered loops must only change by restoring correct evaluation and item selection.
constraints.conceptual: The update should be limited to correcting filtered-loop behavior without changing unrelated template rendering, iteration order, recursion behavior, or fallback behavior.

behavior: Filtered Jinja2 `for` loops evaluate their `if` condition with access to both the current loop target and variables from the enclosing template scope.
Recursive filtered loops no longer fail at render time because of incorrectly scoped free variables referenced by the filter condition.
Non-recursive filtered loops follow the same corrected scoping rules and skip non-matching items without relying on broken render-time scope resolution.
Async template rendering applies the same filtered-loop scoping and filtering behavior as synchronous rendering.
acceptance_criteria: When a template uses a filtered `for` loop whose condition references an enclosing template variable, it should render successfully and include only items that satisfy the condition.

When a recursive filtered loop references surrounding context in its filter expression, it should recurse and render matching descendants without raising `NameError` or a comparable scope-resolution error.
When items do not satisfy a filtered loop condition, they should be skipped rather than causing a render failure or leaking incorrect loop-variable state.
When the same filtered loop is rendered in an async-enabled environment, it should exhibit the same filtering results and scope visibility as in synchronous rendering.

task_4.title: Fix conditional template compilation after known extends blocks
task_4.description: Jinja2 2.9.4 fixes a 2.9.3 regression where templates could compile into invalid Python when top-level output was suppressed after a known extends block inside an if-statement branch, causing template loading to fail instead of treating the branch as a valid no-op.

synthesized_requirement.problem_statement: Ensure that templates using conditional branches around top-level content that becomes silent after a known `{% extends %}` block still compile and load successfully, instead of failing during template compilation.

expectation.grounded: When Jinja2 compiles a template through public compilation paths such as `Environment.get_template` or `Environment.from_string`, any `if`/`elif`/`else` branch whose body reduces to top-level output-silenced content after a known `{% extends %}` must still generate a valid template. Template compilation must not fail with Python indentation-related compile errors solely because that branch emits no executable statements.
expectation.conceptual: Conditional template branches that effectively render nothing because template inheritance suppresses top-level output should still be accepted as valid empty branches. After upgrading, affected templates should compile and render normally instead of failing before render.

constraints.grounded: This fix should only affect branches that become empty during code generation. It must preserve existing rendering behavior for branches that still emit output or perform template actions, and it must not change inheritance or conditional evaluation semantics for unaffected templates.
constraints.conceptual: The change should remove erroneous compilation failures without altering normal conditional behavior, template inheritance behavior, or rendered output for templates that were already valid.

behavior: Template compilation now remains valid even when a conditional branch produces no emitted statements after top-level output is silenced by a known `{% extends %}` path.
Templates that previously failed to load or compile because an `if`-statement branch became empty after inheritance-related output suppression should now compile successfully.
Conditional branches that contain ordinary renderable content or template actions continue to behave the same as before.
acceptance_criteria: Given a template with an `if`/`elif`/`else` branch whose top-level body is suppressed because of a known `{% extends %}` block, when the template is loaded or compiled, it should succeed without raising a Python indentation-related compilation error.
When such a branch is selected at render time, it should behave like an empty no-op branch unless other template content produces output.
When a conditional branch contains normal renderable content or template actions, upgrading to 2.9.4 should not change its rendered output or control-flow behavior.

task_5.title: Make truncate default leeway configurable
task_5.description: The `truncate` template filter now takes its default `leeway` from environment policy configuration instead of a hardcoded value, so applications can globally preserve the newer default behavior or restore older truncation behavior for compatibility-sensitive templates.

synthesized_requirement.problem_statement: Ensure that applications can globally configure the default `truncate` filter leeway so templates remain compatible across versions without requiring every `truncate` call site to pass `leeway` explicitly.

expectation.grounded: When the `truncate` filter is called without an explicit `leeway` argument, it should use `Environment.policies['truncate.leeway']` as the effective default. The environment policy should default to `5`, matching current behavior unless overridden, and an explicitly supplied `leeway` argument should continue to take precedence.
expectation.conceptual: Templates that use `truncate` without specifying `leeway` should follow an application-level default rather than a fixed built-in value. Upgrading applications should be able to keep the newer truncation tolerance or globally restore legacy stricter truncation behavior through configuration alone.

constraints.grounded: This change must not alter `truncate` behavior when callers already pass `leeway` explicitly. Existing validation that the effective `leeway` is non-negative and that the requested length is valid relative to the ending marker should remain in effect. Other `truncate` options, including `length`, `killwords`, and `end`, should retain their prior semantics.
constraints.conceptual: Only the source of the default `leeway` should change. Explicit per-call settings and the rest of the filter's truncation rules should continue to behave the same, and invalid negative defaults should still be rejected.

behavior: The `truncate` filter resolves its default `leeway` from environment policy when the caller omits that argument.
The global default for `truncate.leeway` is `5` unless the application overrides it.
Applications can set `truncate.leeway` to `0` or another non-negative value to globally change when near-threshold strings are left untruncated, improving compatibility with older templates.
An explicit `leeway` passed to `truncate` overrides the environment policy for that call.
acceptance_criteria: When a template calls `truncate` without `leeway` and the environment uses the default policy, the filter should behave as though the default `leeway` is `5`.

When the environment sets `truncate.leeway` to `0` and a template calls `truncate` without `leeway`, strings that exceed the requested length by only the previously tolerated margin should now be truncated.
When a template provides an explicit `leeway` value, the filter should use that value regardless of the configured environment default.
When the effective default `leeway` is non-negative, `truncate` should accept it; when it is negative, the filter should reject it rather than silently applying it.
